newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy Senate approves government austerity budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy Senate approves government austerity budget.

text.p: Italy's upper house of parliament (Senate) on Wednesday approved the centre-left government's 1997 austerity budget, drawn up in a last-gasp bid to prepare for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The controversial package, which aims to slice 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's projected deficit, now goes to the lower house for further ratification.
This second reading is due to be completed by next Monday and if no changes are introduced, the budget will become law.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi told the Senate on Wednesday that once the bill had been fully ratified, his seven month-old government would enter a new phase.

"When we have finished with the budget we must begin the second period of this government, on the one hand looking to reform the institutions and public administration as well as introduce innovations to the justice system," he said.
"On the other hand, we have to work on the economic recovery."

Prodi has fought a bitter battle to get the budget through the Senate, calling four confidence votes in the past three days to push various sections of the complex bill through the house, sidestepping thousands of opposition amendments.

Media mogul Silvio Berlusconi's centre-right opposition bloc has vociferously attacked the package, which leaves welfare spending unscathed and puts much of the emphasis on revenue raising plans, including an unpopular "Euro-tax" levy.

The Freedom Alliance group of centre-right parties, along with the federalist Northern League, have boycotted most of the budget votes, including all the confidence motions as well as the final ballot, to protest against the bill.

"With the approval of the budget in the Senate today...we are closing a session which will be remembered as an ugly page in the history of parliament," said Giulio Maceratini, leader of the hard left National Alliance party in the upper house.
Prodi has said the budget will guarantee Italy a place among founder countries of the single European currency, which is due to be launched in 1999.
He has promised to resign if Italy misses the EMU boat.
However the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on Monday that an expected overshoot in government spending this year would throw Treasury targets out of kilter in 1997.

The budget is designed to reduce the closely watched ratio between Italy's state deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) to 3.1 percent next year, a breath away from the three percent target established by the Maastricht Treaty for EMU aspirants.

The IMF predicted that this ratio would fall to 3.75 percent next year from 7.1 percent in 1996, implying that a mini-budget worth some 14 trillion lire would be needed if Italy was to respect the terms of the Maastricht Treaty.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters on Tuesday that he did not see the need for additional budget measures early next year, but added that the government would do everything necessary to win its EMU bid. ($1=1525 Lire)
